newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico fires drug agents as scandal widens.
newsitem.headline: Mexico fires drug agents as scandal widens.

text.p: The Mexican government fired at least 36 anti-narcotics agents on Monday and warned of more dismissals to come as the latest in a series of drug scandals widenend.
"Right now 36 have been fired, but this is not the last list," Attorney General Jorge Madrazo told reporters.

"Naturally we have detected and removed all those who were in contact at the Institute with Gen. (Jesus) Gutierrez Rebollo," the head of Mexico's National Institute for Combatting Drugs who was fired last week and arrested on charges of working for Mexico's top drug baron, he added.

Madrazo pledged a "very deep" probe of people who had worked with Gutierrez and a wide-ranging evaluation of the damage done to anti-narcotics efforts by his alleged involvement with Amado Carrillo Fuentes, head of the powerful Juarez drugs cartel.
Mexicans, reeling from one big drug scandal after another, agreed on one thing on Monday: news about traffickers' links to top government officals came as no surprise.

Allegations by the New York Times that two state governors were tied to drug lords dominated newspaper front pages just days after Gutierrez's arrest and following sensational stories alleging that former President Carlos Salinas and his family received money and favours from drug lords during his 1988-94 administration.
In each scandal, all of the accused denied strongly the charges against them, but analysts said most of the recent revelations had been circulating as gossip for a long time.

"What are we surprised about?" asked managing editor Raymundo Riva Palacio in a column in Reforma newspaper. After listing a long series of drug scandals going back more than a decade, he said the real problem was "the tolerance, complacency and collusion of the Mexican state with the drug traffickers."

U.S. drug officials say more than 70 percent of the cocaine entering their country comes through Mexico, which is also home to several of the world's most powerful drug cartels and is a major producer of marijuana and heroin.

Diplomats noted that the U.S. and Mexican governments had tried to keep Mexico's failings in the drug war out of the headlines. While the United States has long been happy to lecture Colombia, Peru or Panama publicly about their failings in the war on drugs, Mexico has always received a pat on the back.

U.S. Ambassador to Mexico James Jones never lost a chance to extol the virtues of the Mexican government, laud its commitment to the war on drugs and sing the praises of top officials like Gutierrez and former Attorney-General Antonio Lozano, fired last December amid charges of evidence-rigging and bribery of witnesses.

"What the Clinton administration has failed to understand is that the Mexican system is hopelessly, most likely irredeemably, corrupt," Mexican commentator Jorge Castaneda said in an article for Newsweek magazine.
"The Americans continue to hope that by nudging this rotten giant it will gradually change for the better," he wrote.

Political analyst Jose Antonio Crespo said he thought The New York Times story, which he said appeared to be based mostly on leaks from Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) officials in the United States, might be intended to encourage Zedillo to put more pressure on politicians suspected of drug links.

"I think the United States sees old-guard politicians suspected of links to drug traffickers gaining ground and Zedillo not doing anything about it ... so they put pressure on him to react," Crespo told Reuters.
